What does the handbook require?","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]},"answer":{"text":"An approved car seat.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02"]},"rationale":{"text":"Children under eight need approved car seats unless they are taller than four feet nine inches.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Driving to protect others","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Defensive driving.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Belts and car seats.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the section of additional safety tips. It starts with defensive driving, the habit of staying alert, spotting trouble early, and having a plan, along with the legal duty to shield others from your own errors. Then it turns to safety belts: who must buckle up, which children need approved car seats, the fines for unbelted drivers, riders, and children, and the rule against children riding in open truck beds. Several fine ranges appear here, so we will tie each one to the person it applies to, and to who pays it.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Defensive driving","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay alert with roaming eyes.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},{"text":"Spot trouble early.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},{"text":"Hold a response plan.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Defensive drivers stay alert, keeping their eyes moving. They spot trouble while it is still brewing, early enough to act, and they hold a plan for how they would respond. They also honor a legal duty: to shield other people from their own errors as drivers. So defensive driving has four parts: alert, roaming eyes; spotting trouble early; having a response plan ready; and the duty to protect others from your own mistakes. Defensive drivers stay alert with roaming eyes, spot brewing trouble early, and hold a response plan.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Belts and car seats","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every rider buckles up.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Under eight: approved car seat.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Unless taller than four feet nine.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"All riders in passenger vehicles, pickups, SUVs, and trucks that have belts must buckle up. Children under eight need approved car seats, unless they are taller than four feet nine inches. The handbook gives the reasons: belts prevent riders from being thrown out of the vehicle, prevent them from striking the dashboard, and help prevent loss of control. So the belt rule covers every seat in a belt-equipped vehicle, and the car seat rule covers young children until they turn eight or grow past four feet nine inches, whichever comes first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Fines and open beds","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Unbelted driver or rider: twenty-five to fifty.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Unsecured small child: up to two fifty.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Under-seventeen unbelted: driver pays more.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"An unbelted driver faces a fine of twenty-five to fifty dollars, and the same range applies to unbelted riders fifteen and older. An unsecured small child draws twenty-five to two hundred fifty dollars. A rider under seventeen without a belt costs the driver one hundred to two hundred dollars. A rider under eighteen in an open bed costs the driver twenty-five to two hundred dollars. Children under eighteen may not ride in open truck or trailer beds, though parades, emergencies, rural farm-worker shuttles, beaches, a household's only vehicle, and permitted hayrides are defenses.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Who pays which fine","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driver or rider fifteen-plus: twenty-five to fifty.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Rider under seventeen: driver pays one to two hundred.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Small child: twenty-five to two fifty.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the belt fines. Learners often think the unbelted rider always pays. For riders fifteen and older, the rider faces twenty-five to fifty dollars, the same as an unbelted driver. But when a rider under seventeen goes unbelted, the driver pays one hundred to two hundred dollars. An unsecured small child draws twenty-five to two hundred fifty, and a rider under eighteen in an open bed costs the driver twenty-five to two hundred. When a question gives a rider's age, decide who pays, then pick the matching range.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the car seat","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"A six-year-old, four feet tall.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"What is required?","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a six-year-old who is four feet tall rides in your car. What does the handbook require? Work out your answer before reading on. An approved car seat. Children under eight need approved car seats unless they are taller than four feet nine inches, and this child is under eight and shorter than that. Everyone else in the vehicle buckles up too. Remember that leaving a small child unsecured draws a fine of twenty-five to two hundred fifty dollars, and the belt rule covers every rider in the vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec14-F02","sec14-R01","sec14-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Defensive driving and belts","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alert, early, ready, protective.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Every seat buckles; car seats under eight.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},{"text":"Driver pays for young unbelted riders.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Defensive drivers stay alert with roaming eyes, spot trouble early, hold a response plan, and honor the duty to shield others from their own errors. All riders in belt-equipped vehicles buckle up, and children under eight need approved car seats unless taller than four feet nine inches. Unbelted drivers and riders fifteen and up face twenty-five to fifty dollars, unsecured small children draw twenty-five to two hundred fifty, and drivers pay one hundred to two hundred for unbelted riders under seventeen. Children under eighteen may not ride in open beds except in the listed cases. Next, towed boats and trailers.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-F03","sec14-F04","sec14-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec14-u02","module_id":"sec14-m02","objective_ids":["sec14-u02"],"title":{"text":"Riding in towed vehicles","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The handbook bars young riders from towed boats and bars riders from towed trailers, with a few listed exceptions.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06"]},{"text":"Open beds, towed boats, and towed trailers share a pattern: parades and emergencies excuse most cases.","fact_ids":["sec14-R02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ray plans to tow his boat to the lake with his twelve-year-old nephew sitting in the boat.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Towing a boat with a rider under eighteen aboard is an offense, excused only by parade, emergency, or beach operation.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},"result":{"text":"Ray has his nephew ride in a belted seat in the truck instead.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking adults may ride in a towed trailer as long as children do not.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06"]},"correction":{"text":"Occupying a towed trailer or semitrailer is a Class B misdemeanor for anyone, unless one of the listed exceptions applies.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"No riders in tows.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"When is riding in a towed trailer not an offense?","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"When the tower was unaware, the space suits living in, or the trip is a parade, emergency, farm shuttle, or permitted hayride.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Occupying a towed trailer is a Class B misdemeanor unless one of those exceptions applies; parades and emergencies excuse most of these bans.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"No riders in tow","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Towed boats.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Towed trailers.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers where people may not ride when a vehicle is towing something. The handbook sets a rule for boats and watercraft being towed with a young rider aboard, and a rule for anyone riding in a towed trailer or semitrailer. Each rule has its own short list of exceptions, and the two lists overlap with the open-bed rule from the last lesson. We will look at each rule, its penalty or offense, and its exceptions, then compare all three so you can see the pattern: parades and emergencies excuse most of these cases.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Towed boats","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rider under eighteen aboard: offense.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Excused by parade or emergency.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Or beach operation.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Towing a boat or other watercraft with a rider under eighteen aboard is an offense. The only excuses are a parade, an emergency, or operation on a beach. So the rule is about the age of the rider and the fact that the boat is being towed. Outside a parade, an emergency, or beach operation, a rider under eighteen does not ride in a towed boat. These three excuses are the full list the handbook gives for towed boats with young riders aboard. Towing a boat with a rider under eighteen aboard is an offense outside those three cases.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Towed trailers","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Occupying a towed trailer: Class B.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Unless the tower was unaware.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Or living space, parade, farm, hayride.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Occupying a towed trailer or semitrailer is a Class B misdemeanor. The exceptions are when the person towing was unaware someone was inside, when the space is suited for people to live in, or when the trip is a parade, an emergency, a farm-worker shuttle, or a permitted hayride. Unlike the boat rule, this rule is not limited to young riders; it applies to anyone riding in the towed trailer. So the trailer rule covers everyone, carries a Class B misdemeanor, and has its own list of exceptions, which share parades and emergencies with the other two rules.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Boats, trailers, and beds","fact_ids":["sec14-R02","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Open bed: under eighteen.","fact_ids":["sec14-R02","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F04"]},{"text":"Towed boat: under eighteen.","fact_ids":["sec14-R02","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F04"]},{"text":"Towed trailer: anyone.","fact_ids":["sec14-R02","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from three similar rules. Children under eighteen may not ride in open truck or trailer beds. Riders under eighteen may not ride in a towed boat. And anyone, of any age, commits a Class B misdemeanor by occupying a towed trailer or semitrailer, outside the exceptions. Learners sometimes assume the trailer rule covers only children. It does not. The excuse lists also differ, though parades and emergencies appear in all three. Work out your answer before reading on. When the person towing was unaware someone was inside, when the space is suited for living in, or when the trip is a parade, an emergency, a farm-worker shuttle, or a permitted hayride. Outside those cases, occupying a towed trailer or semitrailer is a Class B misdemeanor for anyone. For a towed boat, the rule is narrower: a rider under eighteen is excused only by a parade, an emergency, or beach operation.","fact_ids":["sec14-F06","sec14-R02","sec14-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Towed vehicles in brief","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Towed boat: no rider under eighteen.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Towed trailer: Class B for anyone.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},{"text":"Parades and emergencies excuse most.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, towing a boat or watercraft with a rider under eighteen aboard is an offense, excused only by a parade, an emergency, or beach operation. Occupying a towed trailer or semitrailer is a Class B misdemeanor unless the tower was unaware, the space suits living in, or the trip was a parade, emergency, farm-worker shuttle, or permitted hayride. Together with the open-bed rule for children under eighteen, these bans share a pattern: parades and emergencies excuse most cases. Next, what to do when a police officer stops you.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec14-u03","module_id":"sec14-m03","objective_ids":["sec14-u03"],"title":{"text":"When police stop you","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08","sec14-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The handbook sets out how to pull over, park, and behave when an officer signals a stop.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08"]},{"text":"Drivers must halt at once for emergency vehicles, with safe options when a spot feels unsafe.","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"At night, Tia sees police lights behind her on a well-lit street.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Drivers pull fully right, park clear of traffic, put the car in park with the brake set, shut off the engine, turn on hazards, and light the dome lamp after dark.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Tia pulls fully to the right, parks, turns off the engine, switches on hazards and the dome light, and keeps both hands on the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you should get out and walk back to the officer to save time.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"Stopped drivers stay seated with both hands on the wheel and exit only when told.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Right, park, off, hands on wheel.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"During a stop, your license is in your glove box. What should you do before reaching for it?","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"Tell the officer where it is first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08"]},"rationale":{"text":"Stopped drivers announce document locations before reaching, keep hands on the wheel, and exit only when told.","fact_ids":["sec14-R03","sec14-F08"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Traffic stops","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pulling over and parking.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},{"text":"Behavior and courtesy.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers what to do when a police officer signals you to stop. The handbook gives a clear sequence: how to pull over and park, what to do with the engine and lights, how to sit and where to keep your hands, how to handle documents and weapons, when to get out, and how to leave when you are released. It also covers courtesy, and what you may do if the place where you are signaled to stop feels unsafe. The steps run from pulling over, through behavior while stopped, to signaling when you are released. Hands stay on the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pulling over","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull fully to the right.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Park clear of traffic; set brake.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Engine off, hazards on, dome lamp.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"When an officer signals you to stop, pull fully to the right and park clear of traffic. Put the vehicle in park and set the brake, then shut off the engine. Turn on your hazard lights, and after dark, turn on the dome lamp inside the car. So the first part of a stop is all about the car: getting it fully off to the right, parked and braked, with the engine off, the hazards flashing, and the inside lit at night. These steps come before any conversation with the officer. Pull fully right, park, and shut off the engine.","fact_ids":["sec14-F07","sec14-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Behavior while stopped","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay seated, hands on the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Say where documents are first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Exit only when told.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Once stopped, stay seated with both hands on the steering wheel, and lower the window partway when it is safe. The officer may approach from either side, and you take directions from whichever side they come. Tell the officer about any weapons. Before reaching for documents, say where they are. Get out of the car only when told to, keep passengers inside, and when you are released, signal before you pull back into traffic. Stay seated, keep both hands on the wheel, and exit only when told. Signal when you are released.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Courtesy and unsafe spots","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Everyone stays seated unless called.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]},{"text":"Hands still until the officer nears.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]},{"text":"Unsafe spot: hazards, call, continue.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Courtesy at a stop means everyone stays seated unless called, hands stay still until the officer is near, and any handgun is stored away from your license and insurance papers. You must halt at once for emergency vehicles, or risk arrest. But if stopping where you are feels unsafe, you may slow down with your hazards on, phone emergency dispatch while complying, or continue to a lighted public place before stopping. So the handbook gives safe options, but none of them is ignoring the lights; each one is a way of complying while getting to a place where stopping feels safe.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F09","sec14-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Halt now or move to safety","fact_ids":["sec14-R04","sec14-F09","sec14-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Emergency lights: halt at once.","fact_ids":["sec14-R04","sec14-F09","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Unsafe spot: hazards and slow crawl.","fact_ids":["sec14-R04","sec14-F09","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"Or call dispatch; continue to light.","fact_ids":["sec14-R04","sec14-F09","sec14-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the stop rules. The handbook says you must halt at once for emergency vehicles, or risk arrest, but if stopping feels unsafe, you have options: slow down with hazards on, phone emergency dispatch while you comply, or continue to a lighted public place. Each option keeps you complying. A second trap is about hands. Tell the officer about any weapons, stay seated, keep passengers inside, and get out only when told. When the officer releases you, signal before you pull back into traffic.
